readerTitle: The car ad that admitted the car was small
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Volkswagen, 광고대행사 Doyle Dane Bernbach의 1959년 'Think Small'과 'Lemon' 광고) + 가상 적용 (소규모 B2B 회사, 주택 도장 업체)
insight: 고객이 이미 보고 있는 약점은 숨길수록 커진다. 먼저 인정하고 그 약점이 고객에게 주는 이득으로 바꿔 말하면 메시지 전체가 믿을 만해진다.
misconception: 광고는 장점만 보여줘야 하고, 약점은 언급하지 않는 것이 안전하다.

sources.text: Advertising Age, 'The Advertising Century: Top 100 Campaigns' (1999): 'Think Small'을 20세기 최고의 광고 캠페인 1위로 선정
Doyle Dane Bernbach (DDB) 회사 역사 자료: 'Think Small'(1959), 'Lemon'(1960) 캠페인, 카피라이터 Julian Koenig, 아트디렉터 Helmut Krone
Volkswagen of America / Volkswagen 헤리티지 자료: 1950~60년대 미국 시장의 Beetle

factChecks.note: 'Think Small' 첫 게재 연도는 대부분의 자료에서 1959년입니다. 1960년으로 적은 자료도 있으니 게시 전에 DDB 또는 Ad Age 자료로 확인하세요.
Ad Age(1999)가 'Think Small'을 20세기 최고 광고 캠페인 1위로 꼽은 사실을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드 3에 이 내용을 적었습니다.
광고 본문이 연료비, 보험료, 수리비, 주차의 이점을 나열했다는 내용은 널리 인용되는 카피에 근거합니다. 카피 속 구체적인 수치(연비 등)는 확인 부담을 줄이기 위해 인용하지 않았습니다.
'Lemon' 광고: 검사원이 글러브박스 크롬 장식의 작은 흠 때문에 차를 불합격시켰다는 내용입니다. 원문 카피로 확인하세요. 검사원 이름은 쓰지 않았습니다.
'1960년대 미국에서 가장 많이 팔린 수입차 중 하나'는 정성적 표현으로만 적었습니다. 판매 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전에 Volkswagen of America 자료로 확인하세요.
광고의 성공에는 차의 실제 경제성과 신뢰성, 판매·서비스망 같은 다른 요인도 작용했습니다. 카드 7에서 광고만으로 성공했다고 과장하지 않도록 했습니다.

cards.title: The car ad that admitted the car was small
body: In 1959, American cars were long, wide and covered in chrome. Car ads made them look even bigger.
Then a magazine page appeared with a tiny car in one corner, a sea of white space, and two words: "Think small." It became one of the most famous ads ever made.

image.label: A tiny car alone on a mostly empty white page
image.brief: 넓은 흰 여백의 잡지 지면 왼쪽 위에 아주 작은 둥근 소형차 한 대. 옆 페이지에는 크롬 장식과 테일핀이 과장된 거대한 1950년대풍 세단 일러스트. 실제 광고를 그대로 재현하지 말고, 실제 로고·엠블럼·상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Sell a small car to people who love big ones.
body: You're the ad agency. Your client makes a small, plain-looking car with an engine in the back. It's cheap to run, but next to American cars it looks odd and tiny. Many buyers have never seen one.
How do you write the ad?

options.text: Use glossy illustrations that make the car look roomy and stylish, like the big brands do
options.feedback: It blends in with every other car ad. And readers can see the car is small, so the ad starts with a claim they won't believe.

options.text: Lead with price: the cheapest new car you can buy
options.feedback: Price gets attention, but it tells buyers the car is a compromise. It doesn't change how they feel about its size.

options.text: Show it small, say it's small, and explain why small is good for the buyer
options.feedback: You give up the dream of looking big. In return, readers trust the ad, because it starts with something they already know is true.

cards.title: Volkswagen said it first.
body: Volkswagen's agency, Doyle Dane Bernbach, ran the Beetle as a small photo on a mostly empty page. The headline was "Think small."
The copy then listed what small meant for the owner: less fuel, cheaper insurance, smaller repair bills, easy parking. The size wasn't hidden. It *was* the selling point.
The Beetle became one of the best-selling imported cars in America in the 1960s. In 1999, *Advertising Age* named "Think Small" the best ad campaign of the 20th century.

image.label: The word 'small' linked to four owner benefits
image.brief: 가운데 "Small" 단어에서 네 갈래 화살표가 "Less fuel", "Cheaper insurance", "Smaller repair bills", "Easy parking" 아이콘으로 이어짐. 단순한 플랫 일러스트, 실제 차량 로고 없음.

cards.title: Own the obvious weakness
body: **Owning the weakness** means naming the doubt customers already have, before they raise it, and then showing what that trait gives them.
It works in two steps. First, admit what's plainly true. That earns trust, because the reader thinks, *they're being straight with me*. Second, reframe: show the benefit hidden inside the weakness.
Hiding a flaw people can see makes every other claim look suspect. Naming it does the opposite.

cards.title: They did it again with one word: "Lemon."
body: In the US, a "lemon" is a car with defects. A later Volkswagen ad showed a Beetle that looked perfect, under the headline "Lemon."
The copy explained that an inspector had rejected this car because of a small blemish on a chrome strip. The scary word turned into proof of how strict Volkswagen's checks were.
Same move as "Think small": say the thing the reader fears, then show why it should reassure them.

cards.title: Every business has a "small."
body: Picture a five-person consulting firm pitching against big names. It can hide its size, or own it:
list: **Small team** → you talk to the people doing the work
**One specialty** → we don't learn on your project
**Newer firm** → we need your reference, so we work for it
cards.callout: Each line admits a fact, then hands the customer a reason to care.
cards.softwareNote: A young app with fewer features can say "It does one thing" and then show why that means setup in minutes, not weeks. Fewer features becomes less to learn.

cards.title: Honesty only works if the reframe is true.
body: Own weaknesses customers already notice. Don't advertise flaws they never thought about.
The benefit must be real and must matter to the buyer. The Beetle's low running costs were real, and the car had to keep delivering them. The ad worked alongside a product that backed it up.
And some weaknesses are dealbreakers. A family of six needing space wasn't won over by "small." Owning a weakness means choosing the customers who value it.

cards.title: Now it's a house painter.
body: Your painting company charges more than most local rivals. You do careful prep and two coats, so the paint lasts longer. Many people get your quote and go quiet.
What do you change in your marketing?

options.text: Stop showing prices and only quote after a home visit
options.feedback: You get more visits, but customers still meet the price later, now feeling ambushed. The doubt hasn't gone away.

options.text: Headline: "We're not the cheapest painter in town," then explain the prep and how long the paint lasts
options.feedback: You lose bargain hunters up front. You win trust with people who hate repainting, and the price now has a reason.

options.text: Match rivals' prices for first-time customers
options.feedback: It may win the first job, but it cuts your margin and tells customers you're just like everyone else.

cards.title: Say the weakness first, then show what it buys the customer.
body: Customers already see your obvious flaw. Naming it earns trust, and the reframe turns it into a reason to choose you.
**Try it today:** write down the one thing customers hesitate about. Write one sentence that admits it, and one that says what it gives them.
